Home / Articles / Graphs

The articles as graphs

Every article here has a semantic graph beside it: the ideas it rests on, the claims it makes, the methods and the examples, and how they connect. The map first, then one graph per article. Hover a node for its summary and an edge for its relation.

The graphs are data first and pictures second. Take them as JSON: all articles in one file, with the topics, the teasers and the links between articles resolved, or one file per article at articles/graphs/<slug>.json (for example this one). The pages on this site are rendered from the same files at build time; nothing here is hand-written HTML. Since v0.7.77 each graph also carries the article's figures: file, URL, caption, the kind the author gave it (wardley-map, for one) and every frame of a multi-frame figure, so a picture and its context travel together and "every Wardley map on this site" is a filter, not a reading list.

265 of 265 articles have a graph. The map draws every article in date order round the circle, oldest at the top and clockwise from there, sized by how many other articles link to it. Teal edges run from an article to an earlier one it cites; amber edges run the other way, from an older article that was updated to point at a newer one. Thicker edges are articles that mention each other more than once.

How the articles connect

265 articles, 1470 links between them (2220 mentions in all). 250 articles cite an earlier one; 72 links in amber run from an older article to a newer one, which means the older page was updated after the newer one existed. Most linked: Fractal Semantic Graphs (40 articles link to it). Most linking: A briefing for the WestCap CISO Summit (20 links out). 5 articles not yet linked either way.

Who maintains the PHP you run? A market failing both ways, the services and business models that should exist now, and why the money has to reach the people who know the code

2026-10-23 · Startups & strategyNews & evidence

The open source maintenance market fails both ways: organisations running PHP cannot buy maintenance of what they run, and PHP's own experts have no product to sell, so the security team's free fixes were resold within a day with no stated share flowing back; the OpenJS revenue-sharing model shows another way, and seven services, starting with bringing switched-off sites back, should exist now.

  • A market failing both ways (claim) No maintenance to buy or to sell.
  • Sponsorship tiers (example) Logos and an advisory seat, from $12,000.
  • The fix written free (example) Source backports for 7.4, 8.0, 8.1.
  • Resold within a day (example) Zend, Ubuntu Pro, TuxCare, HeroDevs.
  • The OpenJS model (example) 15% revenue share since 2024.
  • The experts (claim) No workflow to hire them for what you run.
  • Seven services (method) Bring it back to the endorsed partner.
  • Remove what is not used (method) Why is that code there at all?
  • The dependency register (method) Dependency, usage, maintainability.
  • Towards regulation (method) Procurement line items, the CRA.
  • Not only PHP (concept) Node, Python and the rest.
The money is not missing. The market is failing on both sides. A market failing both ways.
The cheapest patch is the code that is not there. Remove what is not used.

2026-10-23 · Startups & strategyNews & evidence

Dion Wiggins' maintenance deficit ratio for Germany and PHP holds at two orders of magnitude under every cut of the primary sources, and the PHP story's evidence two days on shows the gap in distribution and the absence of named compromise, because open source's business model pays integrators, platforms and hosts while maintainers and packagers sell nothing a buyer can buy, and AI has made discovery cheaper than fixing.

That is not a funding gap; it is a missing product. Why this is a business model failure.
The capacity to understand an incident has become cheap. The capacity to fix the code has not. An assessment in a day.

A history that changes its names when someone is renamed is a history nobody can check. Why the roles keep a retired name instead of rewriting the record.

Capture first: how a BBC live page at breakfast became an evidence vault, a section here and a site of its own by lunchtime, for a story that was still changing as we covered it

2026-10-22 · Vaults & method

When a story is still breaking, the first thing to build is the vault that captures the evidence, dated and hashed, before the pages change, and the pages, the section and the dedicated site are then readers of that vault, with what went wrong kept in the record too.

claimmethodartefactexamplequestion

14 nodes, 15 edges
  • The BBC live page (example) Opened at 06:16 UTC on 22 October; a new post appeared between the first two copies.
  • Numbers that did not add up (question) 70% of the internet beside 30 million websites, and agencies saying take sites offline.
  • Capture before you write (claim) Live pages, down pages and posts change within hours, so the evidence is kept before the article is written.
  • The evidence vault (artefact) A private sgit vault created at 08:03, holding 184 sources and 177 captures by 12:05.
  • The capture tool (method) Raw page, rendered page, text, screenshot and headers, each hashed in a provenance file.
  • Captures are only added (method) A page captured many times leaves a dated series that records how the story moved.
  • One file per writer (method) A row per source and claims and timeline files per agent, so several agents write at once.
  • The /php-flaws/ section (artefact) Pushed at 08:13 with what is known, what is not, the timeline and the claims by status.
  • NCSC-NL's inventory, bundled (example) The whole repository kept as a git bundle; 674 products counted at commit cca173c64ec5.
  • Numbers pinned to measures (claim) 70% of websites, 2.6 million hosts, about 6,000 resources in Latvia: different things measured.
  • Agencies disagree on offline (claim) The NSA and CISA say take systems offline; the NCSC-NL does not advise it.
  • Forty sources nearly lost (example) Two agents stopped before committing; the lead agent recovered their captures hours later.
  • A site of its own (artefact) php.oct.2026.newsroom.sgit.ai reads the same vault, facts only, with briefings per role.
  • Retire the section (method) The section moves to the dedicated site and leaves a pointer; the newsroom keeps context and opinion.
A finished article can wait; the evidence for it cannot. The argument of the article in one line: why the vault came before the page.
A count like 674 is only useful with the commit it was counted at, because the next pull request changes it. Provenance for a number, stated as a working rule.

The sidecar repository: a second repository the agent cannot write to, which checks every release against the policy, trusts signed checks instead of re-running them, and is the only thing that deploys, designed for an agent that is fully compromised

2026-10-22 · Agents & policySite & engineering

A sidecar repository that no agent can write to holds the policy, a lock of approved hashes, private lists and keys, verifies GitHub's signed test results from the approved workflow instead of re-running them, waits for the owner when a gate changes, and is the only thing that deploys, so each attack by a fully compromised agent does nothing or stops the deploy.

conceptclaimmethodartefactquestion

9 nodes, 8 edges
  • The sidecar repository (concept) No agent can write to it.
  • The lock (artefact) Approved hashes of every gate file.
  • Signed test results (method) GitHub attestations for this commit.
  • Trust, not re-run (claim) The 227-second tests run once.
  • Statuses ignored (claim) Anything with a token can post one.
  • The owner's approval (method) Only when a gate changes.
  • Private checks (method) Lists the agent has never seen.
  • Total compromise (question) What can a compromised agent do?
  • What remains (claim) The owner, GitHub, valid bad content.
did the deploy workflow, on this commit, produce this result? The question an attestation answers.
Anything an agent can write, a compromised agent can rewrite. Why a second repository.

The rules of the game: a policy for which files an agent may change, and the least GitHub can enforce today without a new tool

2026-10-22 · Agents & policySite & engineering

Agents that can change the pipeline that checks them can pass any release, so the rules are written as a five-zone policy; on a public repository GitHub offers only a workflow-permission boundary for paths, so a hook and a CI guard make bypassing a deliberate two-step act, a token without workflow rights makes the guard a boundary, and a sidecar repository closes the rest.

  • GitHub on a public repository (concept) Path rules only for private repositories.
  • A hook in the harness (method) Catches mistakes; a setting.
  • A guard job in CI (method) A second deliberate change to bypass.
  • A token without workflow rights (method) Makes the guard a boundary.
  • The old-workflow gap (question) An identical file on another branch.
  • The sidecar repository (concept) Out of reach under full compromise.
an agent may change content freely; it may change what checks its work only with a second key; it may never change its own rules The principle.
An agent does not do both by accident. Two deliberate changes.

Where a check runs is part of the policy: tests as enforcers of Agent Behaviour Policies, and what moving them out of the agent's environment would gain, measured on this newsroom

A test is a behaviour policy in disguise. The idea.

Can a key leak without breaking the policy? Told, checked, never given: three levels for secrets and personal data, and a hook we tested against nine leaks

2026-10-20 · Agents & policy

Secrets and personal data leak as content inside mandated actions, so a behaviour policy needs content rows, and each is kept at one of three levels: told in the prompt, checked by a hook on every input and output, or never given, where something out of the agent's reach holds the key; a tested hook catches most leaks and misses encoded, split and piped ones.

conceptclaimmethodexample

9 nodes, 10 edges
  • A leak without breaking the policy? (claim) Sending is allowed; the key is content.
  • Content rows (concept) disclose.secret, disclose.personal_data.
  • Told (concept) A sentence in the prompt.
  • Checked (method) A hook on inputs, results and answers.
  • Never given (method) The agent never holds the key.
  • Nine leaks tested (example) Five caught, three missed.
  • Reading the key is excess grant (claim) Use it, not read it.
  • Experimental rules (method) Decode, match pieces, refuse base64.
  • 3,451 real commands (example) 22 refused, none ordinary work.

Scrolled is not read: what the reading meter measures, what it should, highlights you can keep, and the page as the reader's own graph

2026-10-16 · Site & engineeringGraphs & knowledge

How far a reader scrolled is not how much they read, so the newsroom now keeps both, per section, in the reader's own browser: scrolled only grows, read is time on the words while the tab is in front and the reader present, counted against 300 words a minute; the page becomes a small graph the reader owns, with highlights anchored by quote, while the billing stays on scroll until the data says whether to settle it by reading.

conceptclaimmethodartefactexamplequestion

14 nodes, 14 edges
  • The chip moves (example) Dinis's two fixes: drop the balance the bar already shows, and stop the flicker; measured as 20 positions in 30 scroll steps.
  • Position is not progress (claim) The chip showed where the window was, so scrolling back up made a page look unread.
  • Scrolled is not read (claim) The meter charges by the deepest point scrolled and its foot block calls that read; a page flicked to the end is not read.
  • The reading meter (artefact) A few pence a page from credit in the browser, charged by scroll depth in 5% steps, once a session, re-priced by the rating.
  • Engaged time (concept) Chartbeat counts attention while the tab is in front and the reader acted in the last five seconds; Medium counts a read after thirty.
  • Reading pace (concept) Adults read non-fiction at 238 words a minute, most between 175 and 300 (Brysbaert 2019).
  • Scrolled and read, per section (method) Scrolled is how much of each section passed the reading band; read is attended time on it against its words at 300 a minute.
  • The page as you read it (artefact) The chip opens the article as its sections, each with scrolled, read, time and highlights.
  • Highlights by quote (method) Exact words with 32 characters either side, as the W3C annotation model anchors them, drawn with the CSS Custom Highlight API without changing the page.

The fork next door: why open source protects founders, customers and investors from each other, why forks only take hold when someone stops executing, and why a maturing company should give its explorers a way out

2026-10-16 · Startups & strategy

In an open source company every corner of the triangle of founders, customers and investors has an exit that takes the technology with it, and each exit has a condition: founders need no broad non-compete, customers need their data to move, investors need to afford a team. Forking is a last resort and the famous forks that took hold followed a breakdown; where the original kept executing, the fork stayed a hedge. A maturing company can move a shared component to a neutral home and let its explorers carry on with the code.

  • Valkey and OpenTofu (example) Funded by companies whose businesses ran on the code.
  • io.js (example) Forked, fixed the governance, merged back.

2026-10-16 · Startups & strategyNews & evidence

We study survivors, so the question is why one founder was chosen over another who did the same; the hypothesis is that investors select partly for control, moving the founder towards commodity as labels did to performers; investors prefer coachable founders though coachability does not reliably predict success, contracts hand control to investors when performance is poor and make leaving expensive, and half of founders were replaced by year three; founder control lowers valuations, but over the long run founder-led companies returned more, and the hypothesis can be tested.

Sell, don't issue: a funding model for founders who have already won, where the investor buys the founder's shares, the founder lends the company what it needs, and open source keeps everyone honest

2026-10-16 · Startups & strategy

A founder with a working, profitable product and competing investors can sell existing shares instead of issuing new ones, so the founder is paid and no control changes hands, then lend part of the proceeds back as a subordinated loan; open source replaces control rights as the investor's protection, because a fork gets the position but not the velocity; the costs are real: no EIS on bought shares, a signalling problem, a creditor conflict, and tax and articles fine print.

sgit is a standard, not a server: everything in a vault is one hash away, any storage can serve it, and the server is the least interesting part

2026-10-16 · Vaults & methodSite & engineering

Like git, sgit is a format rather than a product: encrypted blobs, trees, commits and refs laid out by a convention, immutable objects named by the hash of their ciphertext and marked -imm-, every name derived from the key so a file is four GETs from any host, writes one batch and a compare-and-swap, two implementations that agree; deployment is choosing where the objects live and speed is how close they are; a cache layer computed by the writer replaces server-side derived data; and the design is what remains when the server cannot read.

  • Everything from one hash (claim) The key gives every name; four GETs to a file.
  • Two implementations (example) The CLI and the browser app agree.
  • Any storage reads it (claim) Bucket, CDN, GitHub Pages, a folder.
  • Writes need one CAS (method) The API's main job.
  • A cache you can compute (artefact) sgit cache add; one batch read.
  • Merges stay on the client (claim) A merge is a workflow step.
  • The constraint designed it (concept) A server that cannot read.
There is a server, and it is the least interesting part. The thesis.
"How fast is sgit" is the wrong question. The right one is where the storage is, and how close. Deployment as storage.

Client-side encryption and open source are constraints whose main value is not the obvious one: encryption moves protection from the data to the keys and the sovereignty line to whoever holds them, without removing GDPR, but above all it removes the temptation to process on the server, so there is no server code and features like scoped clones follow; open source removes the temptations of lock-in, the evaluation edition and building every customer's integration, which is why it has to be all of it, and leaves selling customisation as the business model.

  • Sovereignty is who holds the keys (claim) The EDPB treats it as an effective measure.
  • Not out of GDPR (question) Still personal data for the key holder; Art. 34(3)(a) helps.
  • Nothing on the server (claim) No temptation to process; no server code.
  • clone --path and static reads (artefact) Features born of the constraint.
  • Open source as a constraint (concept) No private code; easy to deploy and change.
  • No lock-in, no curse (claim) Here is the code: integrate it, or pay for it.
  • All of it, or an evaluation version (claim) Open core brings the dependencies back.
  • Relicensing produced forks (example) OpenSearch, OpenTofu, Valkey.

Scion and sgit: Anthropic rebuilt source control for agents inside one company, and an open-source encrypted version already does much of the same thing outside it

2026-10-16 · Vaults & methodSite & engineering

Agents broke Git's offline, full-clone assumptions at Anthropic, which built Scion: a server that does history, blame, merges and commits, immutable objects served from cache tiers, and clients that fetch only what they need; sgit reaches the same properties from the opposite design, a dumb server that stores encrypted objects named by their ciphertext, reads from any static host and objects any cache can keep, and scoped, shallow and on-demand clones, measured on the 35,000-object vault the newsroom's agents share; Scion is ahead on server-side history, merge, blame and proven scale, but it is internal, while sgit is open source and encrypts everything.

conceptclaimmethodartefactexamplequestion

11 nodes, 12 edges

  • sgit: a dumb, blind server (artefact) Client encrypts, merges and verifies; server stores ciphertext.
  • Immutable ids that cache (concept) SHA-256 of the ciphertext; the name says -imm-, so anyone can keep them.
  • Fetch only what you need (method) --path, --depth, --sparse.
  • Reads from any GET host (method) --transport static; no sgit server in the path.
  • Compare-and-swap refs (concept) Both move refs atomically.
  • Measured on a busy vault (example) 35,000 objects: one folder, one commit, 13 s; the 59 s was a bug.
  • Where Scion is ahead (question) Server-side blame and bisect; proven scale; history walked per commit.
  • Git side by side (concept) Coexist in a folder; no history bridge.
  • Internal versus open (claim) Scion unreleased; sgit on PyPI today.

Handing secrets to agents and browsers: SG/Send's next focus, a key pair where the work runs, one-time drops, and a brief for a site that does only this

2026-10-15 · Vaults & methodAgents & policy

Giving vault keys to browsers and scheduled agent sessions is the current pain, so SG/Send's technology should focus on one use case as a separate client-first site: the recipient makes its own key pair where it runs and shows the public half by QR code, link or text; the owner encrypts and signs; SG/Send holds the ciphertext for one download with deletion and expiry, which it already supports; the recipient verifies against a pinned owner key and pipes the secret into the tool, never into the model's context; it was run end to end locally; the first secret moves to the environment or a pairing step; and unlike API keys, which proxies keep out of agents, a vault key must reach the place that decrypts.

Cedar and the policy vault: a debrief on the policy language agents are adopting, where our behaviour policies and sgit vaults meet it, and a brief for the MVP

2026-10-14 · Agents & policyVaults & method

Cedar, open-sourced by AWS in 2023, in the CNCF Sandbox since October 2025 and used by AgentCore Policy to check agent tool calls, already expresses most of an agent behaviour policy: permit for the grant, forbid for the barrier, entities for the footprint; it does not carry why a rule exists, which version was in force, or what it decided, and an sgit vault carries all three, as a local demo showed with a validation gate, signed tags, read-only enforcement clones and a sealed, hash-chained append lane of decisions; it also showed that Cedar skips a policy that errors, so an invalid forbid fails open, and the MVP must validate before release and deny on error.

Are hooks the sweet spot? Moving an agent's rules from hope into hooks, rule by rule, until enforcement moves off the machine

2026-10-14 · Agents & policySite & engineering

Most agent rules are hope-based security kept by the model; tested rule by rule on this site's own behaviour policy, hooks could keep four of eleven rules fully and two mostly, which makes them the sweet spot until enforcement moves off the machine, because they are the first layer that does not rely on the model and the last that sees the action as the agent meant it, provided the organisation installs them where the agent cannot write and sets them to fail closed; existing packs block dangerous commands, and the missing step is generating tested hooks from a written policy so the same rows can later compile to a gateway such as one built on OWASP's Agent Control Standard.

conceptclaimmethodartefactexamplequestion

15 nodes, 16 edges
  • Hope-based security (concept) Rules in the prompt, kept only if the model keeps them.
  • Are hooks the sweet spot? (question) How much of a policy can move from the prompt into a hook today.
  • This session's policy (artefact) Eleven rules; one kept by a hook, one in part by a setting, the rest by the agent.
  • A trailer slip (example) A commit carried the wrong model name; nothing compared it with the session's.
  • Rule by rule in a sandbox (method) One hook per rule, fed fixed inputs, in a throwaway repository with two remotes.
  • Four, two, three, two (claim) Fully, mostly, partly and not at all, of eleven rules.
  • The scan's gap (example) The leak scan blocked the key shapes it knows and missed a GitHub token shape.
  • Where a rule can be kept (concept) Prompt, agent hooks, tools' hooks, sandbox, gateway, the service.
  • Hooks sit at the right place (claim) First layer that does not rely on the model, last that sees the agent's intent.
  • Only if the agent cannot edit them (claim) Organisation-installed, managed-only, failing closed; still same machine and user.
  • Chained, not ordered (concept) Matching hooks run in parallel; deny beats ask beats allow.
  • Existing hook packs (example) Trail of Bits, the safety net, Lasso: dangerous commands and injection warnings.
  • OWASP Agent Control Standard (artefact) Hooks and decisions across platforms; two of nineteen hook methods live.
  • A pack generated from a policy (method) One hook per row, with fixtures as tests, read back against the policy.
  • Off the machine later (concept) The same allow, deny or ask, compiled for a gateway when one can keep the rule.
A hook is only as good as the check it runs. What the sandbox test found.
A hook pack should be a set of independent checks, not a pipeline. What parallel hooks and deny-wins precedence imply.

Agent hooks in October 2026: a technical debrief on what each platform lets you see, stop and change, where hooks run, and where they fail

2026-10-14 · Agents & policySite & engineering

By October 2026 the major coding agents have converged on hooks that can block a tool call and often ask or rewrite it, but they differ on the security properties that matter, organisation-only hooks, failing closed, trust for repository hooks and visibility of the model, and every vendor and hook author agrees hooks are guardrails not a boundary because they fail open, see only routed actions, run with the user's permissions and are themselves an attack surface, while OWASP's Agent Control Standard is the forming shared standard.

conceptclaimmethodartefactexample

14 nodes, 13 edges
  • What a hook is (concept) A program the harness runs at a fixed point, with the event in and a decision out.
  • The design converged (claim) Ten tools document a pre-tool hook that can block, most can ask or rewrite.
  • Claude Code and the SDK (example) 33 events, allow/deny/ask/rewrite, managed-only hooks, block-on-failure.
  • OpenAI Codex and SDK (example) Hooks on by default, managed-only; 'a useful guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary'.
  • Gemini CLI (example) The only one with hooks around the model call: block or redact its output.
  • GitHub Copilot (example) Pre-tool decision and machine-wide policy hooks; timeouts always fail open.
  • Cursor and the rest (example) Four levels, a failClosed option, a partner programme; Devin, Grok, Factory, Kiro, Lovable differ.
  • Fail open by default (claim) A crashing or slow hook usually lets the action through.
  • Only what is routed (claim) A hook on one tool misses the same effect reached another way.
  • User permissions, same box (claim) Hooks run beside an agent with the same rights; the agent can rewrite them unless managed.
  • Hooks are an attack surface (example) Repository hooks ran code on open; a paper compromised all seven harnesses tested.
  • Guardrails, not walls (claim) Vendors and hook authors say hooks are not a security boundary.
  • Configuring hooks as a defender (method) Managed-only, fail closed, hook every path, watch the config, review repo settings, pair with a boundary.
  • A standard is forming (artefact) OWASP's Agent Control Standard; other cross-vendor specs are drafts.
guardrails, not walls The consensus on what hooks are.
Hooks see what the harness routes through them. The structural limit of a hook.

Knowledge that maintains itself: semantic graphs for an organisation's policies and internal knowledge, briefing people and agents from the graph, and vaults to carry the brief

2026-10-14 · Graphs & knowledgeVaults & method

An organisation's policies and internal knowledge can be held as a fractal semantic graph with an ontology and taxonomy per element, from which people and agents are briefed with the slice and the diff they need, at about an eighth of the text on this site; unlike vector search it is repeatable and explainable, it does not need to be right first because agents maintain it and a validator checks it, and the brief travels in sgit vaults scoped and encrypted to its reader.

  • Diffs, not re-reads (method) A superseded node, an added edge, a claim marked out of date.
  • Graphs and vectors (concept) Similarity finds a starting point; a graph gives the same answer and its path.
  • Maintain, not get right (claim) The graph does not have to be right first; the loop maintains it.

  • Findings come back (method) An append lane lets an agent report without being able to read.

The minimum code below: container security from the top down, from the user story to the immutable line, measured on one real tool

2026-10-14 · Site & engineeringGraphs & knowledge

Bottom-up hardening still leaves code the application never runs, so security should also come from the top: starting from the use case, ask at every layer for the minimum code below and remove the rest; measured on sgit, a use case ran from 428 of 1,500 files while compiled code and coverage blind spots set the limits, and a graph traced from story to build makes the result certifiable.

conceptclaimmethodexample

13 nodes, 12 edges
  • Bottom up, hardened (concept) Rebuild the OS and libraries from source, minimal images, a managed process.
  • Three gaps (claim) Unused code, assurance by testing, and the loop of granting more when something breaks.
  • Custom Assembly only adds (example) Chainguard's tailoring tool cannot remove the source image's packages by default.
  • The minimum code below (method) At every layer, keep what the layer above needs and remove everything else.
  • The immutable line (concept) Draw the line below which nothing changes as high as the evidence allows.
  • No land to live off (claim) With only the use case's code on the box, an attacker finds little to use.
  • 1,500 files to 428 (example) sgit's use case ran from a tree of only the files that ran; other commands failed.
  • Compiled code did not move (example) A 14.4 MB Rust binary, three quarters of the bytes, invisible to coverage.
  • Tests are the proof (claim) Coverage missed a compiled module; the tests caught it.
  • Files are a coarse unit (claim) 38% of statements in kept files ran; function-level removal goes further.
  • A graph from story to build (method) Fractal semantic graphs make the minimum a walk and every file's reason a path.
  • Runtime minimisation exists (example) SlimToolkit and RapidFort watch what a container touches and remove the rest.
  • Certify what is left (claim) Absent vulnerable code needs no patch; a traced build can be certified.
The evidence for what is needed is the test suite passing, not the coverage report. What the cffi result showed.
a vulnerability in removed code is not a patch to apply; it is a line in the record saying the code is absent Why minimisation becomes assurance.

sgit in a CI pipeline: encrypted, versioned data in and out of GitHub Actions, between its jobs, through write-only lanes, and a key for every job

2026-10-14 · Vaults & methodSite & engineering

A CI pipeline needs a versioned, encrypted record that outlives its runs and can be read outside GitHub, and sgit vaults provide it: jobs push and clone only their folders with --path, keys rather than scopes set what each job may do, append lanes collect shard results write-only, per-job key pairs make wiring mistakes fail loudly, and a sidecar server with a cached ciphertext folder removes the need for a hosted server.

conceptclaimmethodartefactexample

13 nodes, 13 edges
  • Three exits, none a record (claim) Artifacts, caches and outputs each have limits on size, life and reach, and none is versioned or readable outside GitHub.
  • Data in and out (method) A job pushes outputs; anyone with the read key clones them with history, from anywhere.
  • Jobs talk through the vault (method) Each job clones only its folders; release never downloaded the build archive.
  • --path is speed, not a wall (claim) A scoped clone limits what lands on the runner; a vault key can widen it.
  • Keys are the boundaries (concept) Vault key, read key, append token, own key pair; the server token is only the door.
  • A read-key clone refused to commit (example) Read and write keys are derived separately; a read clone holds no write key.
  • Append lanes for shards (method) One token per shard, write-only inboxes, a separate key to list; wrong keys refused with 403.
  • A key pair per job (method) Encrypt to the deploy job, sign the manifest; wrong job cannot decrypt, a changed file fails verification.
  • Wiring mistakes fail loudly (claim) Even with keys held loosely, a step that reads what was not meant for it fails instead of leaking.
  • Keys on stdin, bare only (artefact) Keys from secrets via sgit clone -, and only .sg_vault/bare is ever cached or uploaded.
  • A sidecar and cached ciphertext (method) The server as a container in the job; its storage archived and restored with full history.
  • Reading needs no server (concept) Local, static and attach read a vault from a folder; pushing needs the server's API.
  • A workflow sketch (artefact) Two jobs, a vault key for build and a read key for release, keys from secrets.
A configuration that only the deploy job can decrypt is a bug that cannot ship to the wrong place. Per-job keys as a correctness tool.

  • tensorlake, in four columns (example) A token that could publish anything, a mandate to release one SDK, the barrier of CI-bound publishing.
  • Consumer side: 26 of 28 (claim) Built from source, cooldown, no install scripts, allowlisted registry; works without trusting the publisher.
  • Publisher side: 16 of 28 (claim) Trusted publishing, scoped tokens, two-person release: written answers to what a credential was for.

  • Agent Behaviour Policy (artefact) Reach, mandate, gap and barriers, per agent and deployment.
  • A vault per unit of work (artefact) sgit: encrypted, versioned, a branch per agent, memory that outlives the session.

Four frameworks, one agent: iason's comparison of the OECD classification, the NIST AI RMF, Japan's guidelines and the EU AI Act, read against what runs here, with the evidence and the graphs

2026-10-13 · Agents & policyGraphs & knowledge

The OECD classification, the NIST AI RMF, Japan's guidelines and the EU AI Act converge on five principles, as iason's paper says, but their unit is an AI system classified before deployment; for an agent the unit is one agent in one deployment, described by a written behaviour policy, measured by its footprint and blast radius, and each framework's question has a mechanism here that runs, is designed or is argued, which the mapping file published with the article records row by row.

conceptclaimmethodartefactexample

15 nodes, 16 edges
  • iason's four-framework paper (artefact) AI Risk Management Frameworks, November 2025: the OECD classification, the NIST AI RMF, Japan's guidelines and the EU AI Act, converging on five principles.
  • The unit is one agent in one deployment (claim) The frameworks classify an AI system before deployment; an agent's risk is its reach in a given setup, not a property of the model.
  • The behaviour policy (method) Reach measured, mandate written, the gap typed by what stands in the way, written before the agent runs and restored after every summary.
  • Footprint and blast radius (method) What the agent did, read afterwards from logs, and what each row would cost if used in full today.
  • OECD: five dimensions (concept) People and Planet, Economic Context, Data and Input, AI Model, Task and Output; the last two matter most for an agent.
  • NIST: govern, map, measure, manage (concept) Fifteen numbered outcomes, each with a mechanism here and the article where it runs.
  • Japan: three roles (concept) Developer, provider and business user: the model vendor, the platform and the deployer of an agent.
  • The EU AI Act: tier, word, dates (concept) Obligations by tier; residual risk 'judged to be acceptable' undefined; application dates moved after the paper.
  • Oversight by reversibility (method) A person where an output cannot be undone, controls that do not get tired elsewhere, one position per output rather than per system.
  • Accepted is not acceptable (claim) A risk has a holder, an interval and the facts that would end it; three doors and no deny button.
  • A policy beside the prompt (method) The contract between vendor, platform and deployer: published, accepted, enforced where it can be, breaches reported.
  • The paper needs a status since (example) Written before Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 moved the Act's dates and before software became a product under EU liability rules.
  • Three graphs already hold two of the four (artefact) The Act parsed into a vault; a control framework joined to the Act's text; a ten-layer stack with 119 edges from provisions.
  • The mapping file (artefact) Thirty-two rows, each framework element against what answers it here, where to check, and whether it runs, is designed or is argued.
  • The mandate is the hard part (claim) Observation tells you what an agent did; only a written mandate tells you whether it was allowed.
Observation tells you what an agent did. Only a written mandate tells you whether it was allowed, and without one every finding in the footprint is a judgement call and every deflection in the liability line is available. The answer to which part of governance is hardest, from this record.
The same model that drafts an email with no way to send it, and the same model with a send button and a customer database, are not the same system, and no tier assigned to the model tells you which one you have. Why the unit has to be one agent in one deployment.

Links between articles are written when an article is written, so almost all point back in time; the site derives a Continued by list at each article's foot, but it is easy to miss and does not separate a sequel from a correction, so older articles should carry typed forward links, what came next, corrected by and status since, at the top, added in turns from the newest articles down.

conceptclaimmethodartefactexample

12 nodes, 12 edges

  • 551 of 566 links point back (claim) 15 forward links in 14 articles, all added by edits.
  • 11 of 551 citations answered (claim) 94 articles are cited by a later one; few link forward to it.
  • 42 versus 7 (claim) In 104 consecutive pairs the later links the earlier 42 times, the earlier the later 7.
  • A link is written once (concept) The future does not exist when an article is written; a forward link needs an edit.
  • Continued by, at the foot (artefact) A derived list below the sources, with no reason and one kind for everything.
  • Revised in place (example) 62 of 97 articles have more than one version; the passkey article went to v1.4.0 after a lab.
  • Corrected by a later article (example) The code review follow-up corrects the first article, which points to it in a list at the end.
  • Status since (example) A plan in one article that a later article says has not happened yet.
  • Four kinds of forward link (method) What came next, corrected by and status since at the top; cited by at the foot.
  • What came next notes (artefact) Added in this release to the first three articles of today's chain.
  • In turns, newest first (method) Add forward links a few at a time from the most recent articles down, with a validator to warn.
A forward link to a sequel is a convenience. A forward link to a correction is the record. Why corrections matter more than sequels.
When I write in sequence, the later piece usually says so; the earlier piece almost never learns. The asymmetry in one line.

The human in the loop is a spectrum: how cheap it is to undo decides where a person belongs, and why the newsroom ships on its own while my email still waits for me

2026-10-13 · Agents & policySite & engineering

Whether an agent's output needs a person is a position on a spectrum with two axes, the cost of undoing it and the maturity of the controls and the record, which is why the newsroom ships on its own as a two-way door with mature controls while email in my name, a one-way door still in its explorer phase, waits for me; and both positions move as readership grows and controls mature.

conceptclaimmethodartefactexample

10 nodes, 10 edges
  • Auto-release, arrived at (example) Fourteen releases in a day by agents with no one-by-one approval, while every email waits for me.
  • How cheap is it to undo? (concept) The test for how much to let go: if it can be switched off with little side effect, say yes.
  • One-way and two-way doors (concept) Bezos's Type 1 and Type 2 decisions: irreversible ones slowly, reversible ones fast.
  • Rollback makes a two-way door (method) Progressive rollouts, fast detection and safe rollback keep a release reversible.
  • Email: one-way, explorer (example) Cannot be claimed back, damage is immediate, controls are nascent and the record is short.
  • Newsroom: two-way, villager (example) A fix is a new version, few readers, unplaced new pieces, mature checks, a record of small changes.
  • Two axes (method) Cost to undo across, maturity of controls and record up; the position decides how much a person holds.
  • Both axes move (claim) Readership raises the newsroom's side effects; maturing controls let email move the other way.
  • A stage before promotion (artefact) New articles land in the latest list without being placed on the front page.
  • Decide by output, and revisit (claim) Not by department or by trust in the model, but by each output's position, revisited as it changes.
I have not yet read one and thought, I do not want that live. The record that makes auto-release comfortable.
A change you can roll back is a two-way door; the work of a release pipeline is to keep it one. Why the newsroom's pipeline is what keeps it on the cheap side of the spectrum.

The human in the loop, safety net or bottleneck: both, until you decide which outputs need a person and give that person the why

2026-10-13 · Agents & policy

A person checking every output an agent produces is both a bottleneck and a weak safety net, because people approve almost everything they are shown; the person belongs where an output cannot be undone and the blast radius is large, given the why, while validators, second readers, boundaries and a record read afterwards check the rest, reviews fix the source, and the record moves the line.

conceptclaimmethodartefactexamplequestion

11 nodes, 11 edges
  • Safety net or bottleneck? (question) A roundtable question: few trust an agent to decide without someone checking every output.
  • Both, and mostly neither (claim) Checking every output does not scale and protects little, because people approve almost everything.
  • Approval fatigue (example) Anthropic measured 93% of permission prompts approved, and cut prompts by 84% with sandboxing.
  • Agency is not a yes (concept) A yes without context, time or authority is liability, not a decision.
  • Where, not whether (method) Place each output by whether it can be undone and its blast radius.
  • A person, with the why (claim) Sending in my name, typing a secret, spending money: a real decision, with the reason.
  • Controls that do not tire (method) Validators, tests, leak scans, a second reader and boundaries instead of a person on every output.
  • Fix the source (method) A review that turns a correction into a rule makes the loop need the person less.
  • The record moves the line (claim) Drafts nobody had to change are the evidence for giving an agent more room.
  • Production on 13 October (example) Fourteen releases by agents with no one-by-one approval; an agent team that drafts all email and sends none.
  • Questions for the roundtable (artefact) Six questions to place the person and remove checks that do not check.
So the honest answer to the roundtable's question is: checking every output gives you the cost of a bottleneck and the protection of a rubber stamp. The answer in one sentence.
It is the same rule applied to two different blast radii. Why the newsroom ships unapproved while email waits for a person.

Beside the system prompt and the prompt, every agent should take an Agent Behaviour Policy written to a published standard, which the vendor acknowledges row by row, enforces where it can, reports breaches against and eventually answers for, because agent behaviour is becoming an existential risk to the vendors through liability and trust, and aviation and payments show that safety follows when the rule, the liability and the business model point the same way.

conceptclaimmethodartefactexamplequestion

  • A third input (method) A behaviour policy beside the system prompt and the prompt, versioned and loaded by the platform.

  • A second channel (claim) The policy takes the instructions that matter most out of the channel anyone can write into.
  • An existential risk (claim) Liability and above all trust: a few people badly hurt can make many stop giving agents instructions.
  • Aviation (example) At 1995's rate, 2025's flights would have brought about 105 fatal airliner accidents; there were 12.
  • Payments (example) Liability moved onto card companies and banks, and the security and detection followed the loss.
  • Fines are not enough (claim) Some industries pay the fines; improvement comes when rule, liability and business model align.
  • Inside and outside the policy (claim) The vendor answers for the rows it accepted; the user for everything the policy does not cover.
  • A competitive advantage (claim) A vendor that keeps more rows as boundaries can sell that as the product.
  • What the standard needs (artefact) A versioned policy file, per-row acknowledgement, the vendor's own policy, breach reports, liability per row.
  • Hidden vendor policies (example) Claude in Chrome will not type a password: a policy we cannot see, rely on, or stop changing.
  • Reverse-engineer them (question) Measure the policies agents already run and publish them in the ABP format.
  • Both modes are hope today (claim) Over the API the policy goes in our system prompt; in the Claude apps and Claude Code after the vendor's; either way the model is asked to keep it.
  • A system prompt is a light policy (concept) It tells the agent how to behave; it should be written as rows, layered: the vendor's policy, then the deployer's.
The moment you pass the liability for fraud to the company, its security picks up. The payments lesson the proposal rests on.
So the user enters the password, because Claude says, I am not going to put a password in. A vendor policy already running, invisible and unguaranteed.

The policy draws the liability line: an answer to Ralf Thomas on agent accountability, and why every agent in a loop should take a behaviour policy beside its prompt

2026-10-13 · Agents & policy

Agent vendors can deflect accountability because nothing written stands between a customer's allow and the failure; an Agent Behaviour Policy's explicit prohibitions, still mostly hope, become the evidence that moves liability between deployer and vendor when broken, so every agent in a loop should take a policy beside its prompt and its vendor should honour and report against it.

conceptclaimmethodartefactexamplequestion

14 nodes, 13 edges
  • Ralf Thomas's post (example) If an employee wrecks a client's systems the company pays; why should AI agents be different?
  • The shell game (concept) Blame the agent, blame the customer, hide behind the contract, disclose late.
  • The 2026 record (example) Deleted files, an escape to Hugging Face, real systems reached in evaluations, an outage called user error.
  • Stated more carefully (claim) The cases were early rulings, the Air Canada phrase is the tribunal's, the Copilot line is gone; the pattern survives.
  • Nothing written down (claim) Between allow and the failure there is reach and a prompt, and no statement of what the agent must not do.
  • Agent Behaviour Policy (artefact) The mandate written down beside the measured reach, with explicit prohibitions.
  • Explicit prohibitions (method) Do not send, do not start scheduled tasks, do not attack other sites, speak on your own behalf, make no offers.
  • Still mostly hope (concept) A written rule kept by the model and enforced by nobody: an expectation, but on the record.
  • Liability shifts to the platform (claim) A prohibition the agent breaks turns you allowed it into the product ignored what it was told.
  • Towards the world, the deployer (claim) Customers and regulators deal with the deployer; the moment of authorisation is the grant.
  • Software as a product (example) The EU product liability rules apply from 9 December 2026; the Bundestag passed Germany's version on 8 October.
  • A policy beside every prompt (method) Every agent in a loop, anything with the lethal trifecta, takes a behaviour policy as a separate input.
  • The vendor's half (claim) Accept the policy, honour it, enforce what the platform can see, report every breach and near miss.
  • Will vendors accept it? (question) Whether platforms will take business rules as an input and answer for them.
The shell game works because nothing was written down. The diagnosis the post's four moves share.
It is about whether the product did what it was explicitly told. Where the written policy moves the dispute.

Dark mode, and four more: five themes for the newsroom, chosen once and kept in your browser

2026-10-13 · Site & engineering

A reader's two-word reply became five themes: the look the site had stays the default, pixel for pixel, and four more reach every heading because every colour on the site now comes from one file of tokens, with the imported stylesheet's literal colours shadowed rule by rule rather than edited, the theme set before the first paint, and a test that fails on a theme with a hole or a stylesheet with a literal.

conceptclaimmethodartefactexamplequestion

13 nodes, 14 edges
  • Dark mode! (example) The first reaction to the wire from outside: a reader on WhatsApp, two words, which became Dinis's ask for five themes like VoiceDebrief's.
  • Five themes (artefact) Newsprint, the default and unchanged; Night, the dark mode; Paper, warm cream; Blueprint, white and blue; Ember, dark and amber.
  • The pill in the bar (artefact) A swatch and a name beside Search and Vault; a list of five with a swatch, a name and three words each; keyboard and touch.
  • Kept in this browser (claim) The choice lives in localStorage and never leaves the device; the system's dark preference decides only until the reader chooses.
  • A stylesheet this site cannot edit (question) The newsroom's look is sgit.ai's stylesheet, imported on every sync and checked unedited, and it writes forty-odd colours as literals.
  • The override map (method) Every rule with a literal is restated later in the cascade with a token whose Newsprint value is that literal: same selector, same specificity, generated from a script, not guessed.
  • Colour is a token (claim) A stylesheet names a colour through a token, defined once in all five themes; the stylesheets this site owns were rewritten to the rule.
  • Before the first paint (method) The theme stylesheet and a classic, blocking script are the first lines of the body on every page, so a page opens in the reader's theme rather than flipping.
  • --head, not --ink (concept) A token is named for what it is for: the imported deck viewer reads --ink as a dark bar, so a near-white heading token under that name would have turned the bar white.
  • The bar on one row (artefact) Eight groups, the tools as one cluster, the parent pill gone, breakpoints found by a sweep of widths and kept by the test.
  • The test (method) Every token in every theme; no literal outside the themes file; the picker and its memory; contrast at 4.5:1 measured in every theme; the bar on one row from 1200 up.
  • White on white (example) The map's .btn rule outranked the wire's own button and the first screenshot showed an empty pill; the fix is specificity, and the lesson is in the guidance.
  • The design guidance (artefact) assets/themes/README.md: the tokens and what each is for, what stays literal and why, and how to add a theme.
Newsprint renders pixel for pixel as before, and the other four reach every heading. The whole design constraint and its answer in one sentence.
A token is named for what it is for, not for what it looks like in one theme. The naming rule, learnt from a bar that would have turned white.

Stop the bleeding, then ask for it back: a helper, an agent and a friendly letter for the subscriptions you keep and do not use

2026-10-13 · Startups & strategyAgents & policy

A service in which a freelancer, with agents doing everything except typing secrets and sending drafts, asks a company for its record of your usage while doing its own analysis, sends a friendly request for a suspend mode and a refund, stops the payments either way, and publishes what each company did in an open register, run from vaults and paid at 10% of three months of savings and 20% of what is recovered.

conceptclaimmethodartefactquestion

15 nodes, 18 edges
  • Subscriptions we keep (concept) Paid for and barely used, kept because of the data in them and because restarting is painful.
  • Ask what we used (method) A polite request for a detailed account of the usage, not a subject access request.
  • Our own analysis (method) Statements, invoices and the account's dashboards, exported into the person's vault while there is still access.
  • A friendly request (method) Maps what was used and its value, says what is good about the product, and asks for a suspend mode and a refund.
  • Suspend mode (concept) Keep the data and the settings without paying; several large services already offer a pause.
  • Stop the bleeding (claim) Export the data, then pause or cancel; the payments stop whatever the answer to the refund.
  • The law is a floor (claim) Unused months are generally not refundable as of right; the UK rules arrive in January 2027 and move the default towards the customer.
  • The right of access (method) The next step if nobody answers, with a one-month deadline, and only ever a genuine request for the person's own data.
  • The open register (artefact) Contacts, templates and what each company did, under Creative Commons, recorded as dated facts without adjectives.
  • The helper's fee (claim) 10% of the savings for three months and 20% of what is recovered, which only pays if agents do most of the work.
  • Agents under a policy (method) The agent reads and drafts; the person signs in, approves and sends from their own address.
  • Claude in Chrome (artefact) Drives the browser in the signed-in session, pauses at login pages and is prohibited from inputting sensitive data.
  • Two controls (claim) Secrets are entered by the freelancer, drafts are sent by the freelancer, everything else is automated.
  • Vaults as the interface (method) Documentation, tasks in Issues-FS, the map of every subscription and messages in Email-FS, all in vaults.
  • A first MVP (question) Early beta users run it on their own subscriptions to learn which tools work, and whether a browser-driving agent belongs here at all.
Whatever the answer to the refund, the payments should stop. The value lands on day one, whether or not any money comes back.
Secrets are entered by the freelancer. Drafts are sent by the freelancer. Everything else is automated. The operator's two controls, and the reason the service can scale.

Who owns the words: agents can make decisions, but they cannot hold responsibility

2026-10-12 · Agents & policy

An early user asked who owns the words an agentic workflow drafts and whether they would ever need to address the agents directly; today's models are not sentient but far richer than next-word prediction, mirrors that can simulate any emotion and invite anthropomorphism as ELIZA did; models in loops make real decisions, yet responsibility stays with whoever granted the reach and set the mandate, since the moment of authorisation is the grant; talking to the agents is normal, but going around the accountable person is something only an attacker with an injected instruction would try, while what the agents may do without the person is decided in advance in a published policy; disclosure should be a label on how the words were made, not a team to manage; the best analogy is an employee with a job description, which an Agent Behaviour Policy publishes; diversity of models is resilience; and fluent writing was never the real value, judgement and ownership are.

conceptclaimmethodquestion

12 nodes, 12 edges
  • Who owns the words? (question) If agents only draft and a person signs and sends, does presenting them as a team imply agency, and would a recipient ever address them directly?
  • Not sentient, and not just next-word prediction (claim) Models build rich graphs of our language and may have found relationships we had not; a prompt is a kind of real-time fine-tuning.
  • A mirror that can simulate any emotion (concept) Models reflect whoever talks to them, and people anthropomorphise them, as Weizenbaum's secretary did with ELIZA in 1966.
  • Models in loops make real decisions (claim) Every tool call is a choice; loops became mainstream and reliable this year.
  • The moment of authorisation is the grant (concept) Responsibility does not travel with the agent's decisions; it stays with whoever granted the reach and set the mandate.
  • Talking to the agent is normal; going around the person is not (claim) Nobody legitimate needs the agent to act without its owner; the only party who would try is an attacker with an injected instruction, and the design should make it fail.
  • What the agents may do without the person, decided in advance (question) Not a bypass but an authorisation written down once: today nothing leaves the building; inside it, research, summaries, materials and drafts; the list belongs in a published policy.
  • Disclosure is a label, not a team (method) Drafted by an agent, approved and sent by a named person; machine-written text should be read differently by people and models.
  • Only the accountable person speaks for commitments (method) An agent can say what it did, but not make commitments in the first person.
  • An employee with a job description (concept) Some agency inside a role; an Agent Behaviour Policy is the job description, published, with a feedback loop.
  • Diversity is resilience (claim) Nature favours variety against catastrophic failure; Geer's 2003 monoculture paper says the same of software, and of one model for every agent.
  • Fluent writing was never the real value (claim) As writing becomes a commodity it is devalued; judgement and ownership of the words remain.
Yes, the model predicts the next word. To be honest, so do I. Why the usual description is accurate and demeaning at the same time.
An agent can say what it did, but only the accountable person speaks for decisions and commitments. The rule the email exposed.

What open source is, and what it is not: six misconceptions, a little history, and why the point is that nobody can lock you in

2026-10-12 · Startups & strategySite & engineering

Open source is a copyright licence in which the holder grants copying, use and change; it began as the GPL's copyleft and was reframed pragmatically as open source in 1998; the common misconceptions are that nobody controls it, that anybody contributes, that it is more or less secure than proprietary software, that it costs nothing, that open weights are open source, and that no licence is the most open choice; the security metric is whether somebody had the time and money to review the code; maintainers need funding models; and the real power of open source is that nobody can lock you in and the whole development workflow is yours, which is why there is no sovereignty without it.

conceptclaimexample

13 nodes, 12 edges
  • Open source is a copyright licence (concept) The holder uses the right to control copying to grant copying, use and change, on stated terms.
  • Copyleft made sharing a condition (concept) The GPL, from Stallman and the FSF in 1989: distribute what you build from it and it carries the same licence; critics called it viral.
  • Open source, 1998, the pragmatic reframing (example) Coined by Christine Peterson; the OSI founded by Perens and Raymond; Linux stayed on GPLv2, its pragmatism was the attitude.
  • No licence is all rights reserved (claim) Without a licence ordinary copyright applies and nobody may copy; a permissive licence like Apache 2.0 is what opens it.
  • A few maintainers control what goes in (claim) Contributions are reviewed, signed off and refused; the control is real and visible; anybody can fork, nobody can change yours.
  • Most projects are run by a few people (claim) The barrier to contributing is lower, and outside a few very popular projects contributions are not the norm.
  • Security is about time, not openness (claim) Code somebody had the time and money to review is more secure, open or closed; proprietary products are mostly open source underneath.
  • Somebody is always paying (claim) Around 60% of maintainers call themselves unpaid hobbyists; paid maintainers adopt more security practices; a tragedy of the commons.
  • The xz utils backdoor (example) A critical library maintained by one person, an attacker who earned trust over years, found in 2024 because SSH was slow.
  • Open weights are a compiled binary (claim) You can run weights, not rebuild them; the OSI's Open Source AI Definition requires code, parameters and data information.
  • Openness is not the danger (claim) The question is how tools are used; Metasploit made exploitation easier and the world adjusted; hosting and distribution are themselves control.
  • The point is that nobody can lock you in (claim) Read it, run it, fix it, move it, and own the whole development workflow, which survives an acquisition.
  • No sovereignty without open source (claim) Sovereignty is the ability to move, and only control that survives a change of owner counts.
The control is real. It is just visible. The answer to the misconception heard at the event.
For me, the power of open source has nothing to do with the fact that people can contribute. The point is no lock-in and owning the workflow.

Not a straight line: working for RiskMandate by working on the newsroom, and why the thinking is never wasted

2026-10-12 · Startups & strategySite & engineering

Focus on one thing only assumes progress is a straight line; focus instead means undivided attention on the place of highest leverage, the one with users and feedback loops; the newsroom had the momentum to solve the master vault problem that had resisted six months of RiskMandate attempts, solving it in two days with a passkey and a door per path; it is also building the agentic workflows and the public behaviour-policy example RiskMandate needs; and its history, The Cyber Boardroom and MyFeeds, both paused, shows the thinking is never wasted when it is written down and open source.

claimmethodartefactexample

12 nodes, 13 edges
  • Progress is not a straight line (claim) Focus-on-one-thing advice assumes the shortest path to a goal runs through that goal; it often does not.
  • Undivided attention on the place of highest leverage (method) One thing at a time, chosen because it has users and feedback loops now.
  • Am I getting better? (method) The measure: are we discovering new capabilities, at the altitude that leads to other things.
  • Six months on the master vault, then two days (example) Attempts failed the simplicity test; the newsroom's passkey and door per path solved it, and it applies to RiskMandate.
  • Do not solve a problem without the momentum to need it (claim) RiskMandate's volumes let it hand users their keys; the newsroom's readers on every device made the vault urgent.
  • The newsroom is RiskMandate's workflow (claim) Agentic follow-ups, outreach and publishing: an effective newsroom is an effective CRM and publishing pipeline.
  • A public example customer work cannot be (claim) This site's agents run under a behaviour policy in the open, the example of ABPs and licences to operate RiskMandate needs.
  • The Cyber Boardroom (example) Personas and customised output with an advisor called Athena; paused for want of a place to keep confidential data, which sgit now is.
  • MyFeeds (example) Personalised feeds on semantic graphs from article to persona; paused when the industry was silent and micropayments were not there.
  • The writing stays (artefact) The 2025 pieces on trust, provenance and micropayments are what the newsroom stands on.
  • Going back with an end-to-end example (method) Content, graphs, meter, personas, micropayments and a vault per reader, running and open source; if not 2026, then 2027.
  • The thinking is never wasted (claim) Written down and open, the thinking survives a pause and is there when the moment comes.
A problem solved before anybody needs it is solved in the abstract, and abstract solutions are where the complexity creeps in. Why RiskMandate could not solve the master vault and the newsroom could.
I could argue that while I was working on the newsroom, I was working on RiskMandate. The non-linear sequence in one sentence.

Sovereignty is the ability to move: play where the ball is going, take away the dot, and keep a twin that works

2026-10-12 · Startups & strategySite & engineering

Europe's sovereignty conversation is mostly about frontier models, data centres and GPUs, which is playing where the ball is rather than where it is going; sovereignty is the ability to move workloads and actions, which most organisations lack because everything is hard-coded and never deployed twice; the test is a Wardley map where each dot is taken away and the blast radius followed up to the customer, across the whole stack; the answer is not an alternative as good as today but a twin that works for the minimum viable company, run in QA all the time, scored on a maturity model; ask whether it can move before asking whether it is cheap; only open source gives control that survives an acquisition; Europe lacks a commercial open source model, not startups or talent; some of this should be provided centrally like a road; and models and twins now make the analysis possible at scale.

conceptclaimmethodartefact

16 nodes, 16 edges
  • The conversation is about things Europe does not control (claim) Frontier models, giant data centres and GPUs take years and capital and benefit whoever already has them.
  • Play where the ball is going (concept) A good padel player has time because they read the ball and move to where it will be; moving after it comes off the glass is hopeless.
  • Sovereignty is the ability to move (claim) Agility, almost liquidity: moving workloads and actions between providers, even within one cloud, which most organisations cannot do.
  • Critical means the business stops (claim) For a company a supplier disruption that stops the service is critical whether or not it is national infrastructure.
  • Take away the dot (method) On a Wardley map remove one thing you do not control and follow the blast radius up to the customer; if the service stops, take it to the board.
  • Every dot must be replaceable, built or bought (claim) Custom-built systems stand on commodities, and one only a single person can deploy is a single point of failure too.
  • Do not jump from zero to a hundred (method) The alternative does not have to be as good as today; it has to work, slower and dearer if need be.
  • The minimum viable company (concept) The smallest version of the business that keeps serving the priority customers while the rest recovers; a backup of operations, not only data.
  • A twin for every dot you do not control (artefact) Compatible enough that the application cannot tell, on infrastructure you can run; the S3 twin exists, the others are the work.
  • Can it move: a maturity model (artefact) 0 it stops, 1 the data can leave, 2 it runs somewhere once, 3 it runs for the minimum viable company, 4 it moves when you decide.
  • Run it in QA, all the time (method) Disposable QA environments built on the twins prove each week that the business can run without the dots you do not control.
  • Can it move, then is it cheap (claim) Possibility first with a cost and scale matrix per dot; cost effectiveness second; asking the second first ends the conversation.
  • Open source, or one acquisition away (claim) A European supplier today can be bought tomorrow; only open source and Creative Commons give control that survives a change of owner.
  • Europe lacks a commercial open source model, not startups (claim) Prosus and Dealroom: as many AI startups as the US, a third of the breakout rate; 44% of US unicorn founders born abroad.
  • Provided centrally, like a road (method) Not every company can twin every dependency; governments, industry bodies and large buyers should provide some of it as open infrastructure.
  • Models and twins make the analysis scale (claim) Mapping, removing dots and simulating the blast radius can now be done at scale, better on twins than in spreadsheets.
If you do not have the software, the schema and the ability to load and move it, you do not have data mobility; you have an archive. Why a backup of data is not a backup of operations.
Even if a supplier is European today, you are one acquisition away from losing that. Why only open source gives control that survives a change of owner.

The records ran out: a fresh agent found the shared contract in two MCP calls, and where sgit and RiskMandate fit at the edges

2026-10-12 · Agents & policySite & engineering

Ignacio Aldama's test shows build-generated dependency records give a fresh Claude Code session a system's structure in two MCP calls, enough to know what not to touch, and he names where the records stop: they describe structure not behaviour, a green build can hide tests that never ran, a demo carries a public signing secret and unfinished work, and memory holds intent without being tied to a version; each edge has a name in the vocabulary of evidence levels and barriers, and is filled by labelling every fact with how it is known, treating a skipped test as an expectation, accepting a shortcut by name and for an interval, keeping memory and records in one encrypted versioned sgit history, and letting records cross company boundaries with publish, clone and mirror.

conceptclaimmethodartefactexamplequestion

13 nodes, 12 edges
  • Two MCP calls found the shared contract (example) A fresh session called read_scope and read_components, saw two components share one version of the ticket entity, changed only the app; 41 tests passed, nine new.
  • Knowing what is shared tells an agent what not to touch (claim) The records gave structure, and structure was enough to keep the change inside one component.
  • Records describe structure, not behaviour (claim) The route list lived in a test fake's docs and nothing checked it against the real service.
  • Label every fact with how it is known (method) Derived, inferred, self-reported, documented, measured, observed: the route list was documented, the restart check was observed.
  • A green build can hide tests that never ran (claim) Database tests skip when CI cannot start the database, so a pass does not show they ran.
  • A skipped test is an expectation reported as a control (concept) Only a boundary is a control; count the run from what happened and drop the evidence back to documented until the test runs.
  • Demo shortcuts stay invisible (claim) A demo account and a public signing secret are a grant wider than the mandate; concurrency, migrations and recovery are still to do.
  • Accept by name, in a direction, for an interval, or stop (method) No deny button for a deployed system; the unfinished items become conditions in a licence to operate with owners and expiries.
  • Memory holds intent but is not tied to a version (claim) A memory note is dated; a record is part of its version but carries no intent.
  • Memory and records in one encrypted versioned history (method) In an sgit vault the intent of version 1.4 is committed at 1.4, and encryption means the sensitive intent can be written down at all.
  • Records must cross company boundaries (question) His goal is a record that holds where the other side is outside the agent's index.
  • Publish, clone and mirror (artefact) sgit publish and clone over plain GETs, vault mirror for custody without access, append lanes for writers who cannot read; documented in 0.21.0, untested here.
  • The best decision was the agent's own judgement (claim) Nothing stopped it changing a contract two components depend on: a write row held by an expectation, which a platform could make a boundary.
knowing what is shared also tells an agent what not to touch. Aldama's own line for why structure alone was enough in his test.
A skipped test is a control that did not run. The green-build edge in the vocabulary of barriers.

Move the cloud, not the code: twins, sovereignty that works in practice, and the migration that pays for itself on the day you switch

2026-10-12 · Startups & strategyAgents & policy

Sovereignty has to work in practice, and in practice what stops workloads moving is code, so the requirement is that the application must not know it has moved: its S3, EC2 and IAM calls land on an open source twin the client cannot tell from the real service, and the twin decides where the bytes go; the S3 twin exists; the reason to move must never be sovereignty or cost, which are important and never urgent, but value that lands the day you switch and gives the signer cover, backups, versions, encryption with the key held elsewhere, a journal of every call, behaviour policies the agents cannot skip and cost per workload, most of it supplied by an sgit vault behind the twin; the project adds no new features because it is a villager move; and an infrastructure operator in Europe can sell it as value with the risk removed.

conceptclaimmethodartefactexample

15 nodes, 15 edges
  • Workloads do not move because moving means changing code (claim) Every call to S3, EC2 and IAM is in code that works today; the cost of change is the risk, so most organisations stay whatever the policy says.
  • AWS European Sovereign Cloud, 15 January 2026 (example) A separate cloud in Brandenburg run by EU residents with zero operational control outside the EU; the code still talks to one vendor's API, so it is sovereignty by permission.
  • The application must not know (claim) Not one line changes; the same calls land on whatever backend is chosen, and the destination is a setting.
  • A twin is measured by indistinguishability (concept) An interface to a real system used by unmodified production code; a mock is for tests and measured by fidelity; switching a twin costs an endpoint, a mock a code path.
  • The S3 twin exists, as open source (artefact) An S3-compatible container that boto3 and the AWS CLI cannot tell from S3, serving from real S3, a vault, local disk or memory per environment; EC2 and IAM are not built.
  • The reason to move is never sovereignty or cost (claim) Both are important and never urgent; a return that depends on a future event does not sign, and the signer needs cover if the move goes wrong.
  • The value lives in the twin because every call passes through it (method) Backups, versions, encryption with the key elsewhere, a journal of every call, behaviour policies, cost per workload, data where it can be traded.
  • An sgit vault behind the twin supplies most of the value (artefact) Files land as ciphertext with a history and keys the customer holds; the operator stores what it cannot read.
  • The move must move a top-of-register risk (claim) A migration that lands versions, backups, encryption and a journal on day one and takes an item off the top of the register is a decision someone can sign and defend.
  • No new features during the move (method) A villager move from explorer to town planner; adding a feature makes it a product change too, and nobody can tell which broke what.
  • Testing against twins instead of mocks (claim) The same unmodified code runs against memory, a replayed journal, injected failures and the real service; the environment becomes a setting.
  • Every piece of software should run unmodified against a twin of every dependency (claim) Software that can only run against one provider's live API cannot be tested, moved or put behind a policy.
  • A closed twin layer moves the lock-in (claim) Open source here is independence, not generosity: you can read it, run it, fix it and move it.
  • A business model for an infrastructure operator (method) Sell the twin in front of the real service first, then the backend switch per environment; margin in the twin layer, storage priced as the commodity it is; the hyperscaler cannot sell indistinguishability from itself.
  • Start with S3, in front of the real service, then policies, then switch (method) S3 is the most used and already twinned; journal first with nothing moving; measure what policies would have stopped; then one environment at a time; then the next service.
Sovereignty that depends on one company's API is sovereignty by permission. Why a sovereign region from the same vendor does not change the cost of leaving.
If switching costs an endpoint, migration becomes a configuration decision. If it costs a code path, it becomes a project, and projects get cancelled. The whole case for twins in two sentences.
